title: Amsterdam
hook: Spanish and Portuguese Jews rebuild open Jewish life in Amsterdam

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ghetto in Venice. Your line was walls around people. Did you notice a wall today, built or invisible? Now we travel north, to a city of canals where the walls came down. Day nine hundred fifty-seven.

A grown man sits at a table with a teacher half his age, sounding out Hebrew letters like a child. His family has carried a secret for generations: clean linen laid on the beds every Friday, a grandmother who refused pork without ever saying why. Back in Portugal, saying more could have cost them everything. Here, in a port city of canals and warehouses, he can say it out loud. He is a Jew. Now he has to learn what that means. Today, the city where he learns it.
screen: `A GROWN MAN LEARNING HIS LETTERS.` → `A FAMILY SECRET.` → `NOW HE CAN SAY IT OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: After the expulsions from Spain and Portugal, some Jewish families stayed and were baptized, by force or under heavy pressure. Some of them kept Jewish customs in secret, and the Inquisition hunted for exactly those signs. Over time, some of these families slipped away, and a number of them reached Amsterdam, a trading city where they could live openly as Jews. Getting out was dangerous. Arriving brought a different problem: much had been forgotten. Some had never seen a Torah scroll or heard the prayers in Hebrew. So the newcomers set to work. They rebuilt Jewish life almost from the ground up. They brought in rabbis and teachers from other communities. They founded congregations and schools. Grown men chose to be circumcised. Prayer books and teachings were printed in Spanish and Portuguese, the languages people actually spoke, so they could find their way back. They called themselves a nation, and they governed their community with care, with elders who set rules and kept the peace. There is an old letter in the Tanakh that fits them. The prophet Jeremiah writes to Jews carried off to Babylon, far from home, and tells them not to wait with their bags packed: "Build ye houses, and dwell in them." Plant gardens. Raise families. Seek the peace of the city where you live. Amsterdam is that letter lived out. A new home, built on purpose. And an old faith, rebuilt piece by piece, by people who had nearly lost it and decided to learn it again.
screen: `BAPTIZED, BUT KEEPING SECRETS.` · `A CITY WHERE THEY COULD BE OPEN.` · `RELEARNING ALMOST EVERYTHING.` · `BUILD YE HOUSES, AND DWELL IN THEM.` · then, large: `NEW HOME, OLD FAITH.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: rebuild one thing. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Think of something you once had and let slip. A habit of prayer or quiet. A friendship. A language you used to speak. A song your family sang. Don't judge how it slipped away. Just hold it for a moment. Then ask: what is one small piece of it I could pick up again this week? One letter, one phone call, one verse. If you pray, you can ask for help in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Amsterdam. The trading city where Spanish and Portuguese Jews, some returning from secret lives, rebuilt open Jewish life. Today's word.
Your line: new home, old faith. Today, take one step toward something you let slip: one call, one page, one old song. Day nine hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Spanish and Portuguese Jewish congregations, including in Amsterdam, keep their own melodies and customs, and their members often tell the story of ancestors who returned to open Jewish life after living in secret.
